newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan guru to face followers in murder trial.
newsitem.headline: Japan guru to face followers in murder trial.

text.p: Doomsday cult leader Shoko Asahara, whose trial for the poison gas attack on the Tokyo subway last year resumes on Thursday, is to be confronted by his followers in court.

Asahara, 41, will appear in Tokyo District Court accused of ordering followers to release the deadly nerve gas sarin on rush-hour subway trains in March 1995. The attack killed 11 people and made 5,500 ill.
The case resumes after a summer recess on Thursday, when the court will hear from subway employees and police officers who removed sarin-filled plastic bags from the trains on the day of the attack.

But the highlight of testimony by prosecution witnesses comes later this month, with a confrontation between Asahara, whose real name is Chizuo Matsumoto, and his disciples in Aum Shinri Kyo (Supreme Truth Sect), which the guru founded.

The sect's doctor, Ikuo Hayashi, and Asahara's lieutenant Yoshihiro Inoue, both accused of taking part in the subway attack, will testify on the role Asahara played in the gassing in court hearings set for September 19 and 20.
Two other former disciples on trial will confront Asahara in court hearings set for October.
In their court appearances, most followers have blamed Asahara for ordering gassings, weapons production and murders which kept Japan in a state of near panic for months last year.

But with the court sessions moving at a snail's pace, public interest is waning. In contrast with April, when some 12,000 people queued for a seat at the first hearing in Asahara's trial, in a July hearing only a few hundred appeared.
Security will remain tight, with several prime suspects still at large, but the scale will not equal that of April.

One factor delaying court proceedings, aside from the scale and complexity of the crimes, is the court-appointed defence lawyers' determination to scrutinise every legal detail before having Asahara enter pleas.

Asahara's lawyers, who have objected to most of the 15,000 pieces of evidence submitted by the prosecutors, will submit on Thursday a list of 250 questions on the evidence for the prosecutors to clarify.

The lawyers also indicated to reporters on Wednesday that Asahara is not expected to enter pleas to the 17 charges, which include the murder of an anti-cult lawyer and his family, drug and ammunition manufacturing and kidnap of former followers.
Asahara refused to enter pleas in the previous hearings.
In contrast with the criminal court case, which is expected by jurists to take more than 10 years to complete, related legal proceedings are moving more quickly.

On Monday, Tokyo District Court ordered Asahara and two of his lieutenants to pay damages to the victims and families of those killed in the subway gas attack after the three failed to present a defence against the suit.
The suit was filed last October by a 38-member group of victims and relatives of those who died in the gas attack.
Authorities are also expected to reach a decision on whether to outlaw the cult in the next few months.
The Public Security Commission is now considering a request by the Public Investigation Agency, an arm of the Justice Ministry, to outlaw the sect under the 1952 Subversive Activities Prevention Law.
